Anatomy-03.question: ১) What term applies to collections of neuronal cell bodies (somata) outside the central nervous system?
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is ganglia. Ganglia are collections of neuronal cell bodies (somata) located outside the central nervous system (CNS).

Key points:

  • Ganglia → Collections of neuron cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system (PNS)

  • Examples:

    • Dorsal root ganglia

    • Autonomic ganglia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neuroglia 

    • Supporting cells of the nervous system (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, etc.).

  • Nodes 

    • Refers to structures like nodes of Ranvier, gaps in myelin along axons.

  • Nuclei 

    • Collections of neuronal cell bodies within the CNS (brain and spinal cord).

High-yield neuroanatomy:

Location Collection of neuron cell bodies
Outside CNS (PNS) Ganglia
Inside CNS Nuclei

Exam pearl:
Neuron cell bodies outside CNS = Ganglia.

Anatomy-03.question: ২) The structures providing structural support to astrocytes -
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is intermediate filament. Astrocytes contain glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), which is an intermediate filament that provides structural support and maintains the shape of astrocytes.

Key points:

  • GFAP → Intermediate filament → Astrocyte structural support

  • Used as a marker for astrocytes in histology and neuropathology

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Microfilaments → Mainly involved in cell movement and contraction (actin-based).

  • Microtubules → Involved in intracellular transport and maintaining cell polarity.

  • Secondary filament → Not a recognized cytoskeletal component.

High-yield neurohistology:

Cytoskeletal component Main role
Intermediate filament (GFAP) Structural support in astrocytes
Microtubules Axonal transport
Microfilaments Cell motility

Exam pearl:
Astrocyte marker and structural filament = GFAP (intermediate filament).

Anatomy-03.question: ৩) Neuroglial cell take part in formation of blood-brain-barrier
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is astrocyte. Astrocytes play an important role in the formation and maintenance of the blood–brain barrier (BBB).

Functions of astrocytes in BBB:

  • Astrocyte end-feet surround cerebral capillaries

  • Support tight junctions between endothelial cells

  • Regulate exchange of substances between blood and brain tissue

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Oligodendrocyte → Forms myelin sheath in the CNS.

  • Ependymal cell → Lines ventricles and helps form the choroid plexus; involved in CSF production.

  • Satellite cells (of ganglia) → Support neurons in peripheral ganglia.

High-yield neuroglia:

Cell Main function
Astrocyte Blood–brain barrier support, repair, ion regulation
Oligodendrocyte CNS myelin formation
Microglia Phagocytosis/immune defence
Ependymal cell CSF production and ventricular lining

Exam pearl:
BBB formation and maintenance = Astrocyte end-feet.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪) Arachnoid and pia mater together called
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is leptomeninges. The arachnoid mater and pia mater together are called leptomeninges.

Meninges of the brain and spinal cord:

  1. Dura mater

    • Outer, tough fibrous layer

    • Called pachymeninx

  2. Arachnoid mater + Pia mater

    • Inner delicate layers

    • Called leptomeninges

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pachymeninx → Refers to dura mater only.

  • Filum terminale → Fibrous extension of pia mater anchoring the spinal cord to the coccyx.

  • Cauda equina → Bundle of lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal nerve roots below the conus medullaris.

High-yield meninges:

Term Components
Leptomeninges Arachnoid + Pia mater
Pachymeninx Dura mater

Exam pearl:
Arachnoid + pia = Leptomeninges.

Anatomy-03.question: ৫) Foramen of Monro connects:
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is lateral ventricle to third ventricle. The foramen of Monro (interventricular foramen) connects each lateral ventricle with the third ventricle, allowing cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow.

CSF pathway:

Lateral ventricle
→ Foramen of Monro
→ Third ventricle
→ Cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius)
→ Fourth ventricle

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Lateral ventricle to 4th ventricle → No direct connection.

  • Third ventricle to 4th ventricle → Connected by the cerebral aqueduct, not foramen of Monro.

  • Third ventricle to aqueduct → This is the role of the cerebral aqueduct.

High-yield CSF pathway:

Structure Connection
Foramen of Monro Lateral ventricle → Third ventricle
Cerebral aqueduct Third ventricle → Fourth ventricle

Exam pearl:
Foramen of Monro = interventricular connection between lateral and third ventricles.

Anatomy-03.question: ৬) Spinal cord gives rise to ______of spinal nerves
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is 31 pairs. The spinal cord gives rise to 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

Distribution of spinal nerves:

Region Number of pairs
Cervical 8 pairs
Thoracic 12 pairs
Lumbar 5 pairs
Sacral 5 pairs
Coccygeal 1 pair
Total 31 pairs

The other options are incorrect because they do not represent the normal number of spinal nerve pairs.

Exam pearl:
Spinal nerves = 31 pairs (8C + 12T + 5L + 5S + 1Co).

Anatomy-03.question: ৭) Which layer of meninges is tough?
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is dura mater. The dura mater is the toughest and outermost layer of the meninges.

Layers of meninges (outer → inner):

  1. Dura mater

    • Thick, tough, fibrous connective tissue

    • Provides strong protection to the brain and spinal cord

  2. Arachnoid mater

    • Thin, web-like middle layer

    • Contains the subarachnoid space with CSF

  3. Pia mater

    • Delicate inner layer

    • Closely follows the surface of the brain and spinal cord

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Arachnoid mater → Thin and delicate, not tough.

  • Pia mater → Very thin vascular membrane.

Exam pearl:
Toughest meningeal layer = Dura mater.

Anatomy-03.question: ৮) Multipolar neuron
Anatomy-03.exp:
Multipolar: Motor neurons, autonomic neurons,  Peripheral nerves, CNS pyramidal cells/interneurons
Unipolar: Adult human-এ rare

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Sensory cochlea → Contains bipolar neurons (spiral ganglion cells).

  • Posterior root ganglion (dorsal root ganglion) → Contains pseudounipolar neurons.

  • Peripheral nerves → Mainly contain axons, not multipolar neuronal cell bodies.

High-yield neuron types:

Neuron type Example
Multipolar Retinal ganglion cells, motor neurons, interneurons
Bipolar Retina (photoreceptors pathway), cochlear and vestibular ganglia
Pseudounipolar Dorsal root ganglion

Exam pearl:
Multipolar neuron = Retina (ganglion cells) and motor neurons.

Anatomy-03.question: ৯) Basal nuclei exclude
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is vermis. The vermis is a part of the cerebellum, not a basal nucleus.

Components associated with basal nuclei (basal ganglia) include:

  • Corpus striatum

    • Caudate nucleus

    • Putamen

  • Amygdaloid nucleus

  • Claustrum (often grouped with basal forebrain structures)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Corpus striatum → Major component of basal nuclei.

  • Amygdaloid nucleus → Considered part of basal nuclei in many anatomical classifications.

  • Claustrum → Thin sheet of grey matter associated with basal nuclei.

High-yield neuroanatomy:

Basal nuclei = Corpus striatum + Amygdala + Claustrum
Vermis = Cerebellar structure

Exam pearl:
Structure not belonging to basal nuclei = Vermis.

Anatomy-03.question: ১০) Golgi type-2 neuron
১১) Neuroglial cell of monocyte origin
১২) Neuroglial cell located in peripheral nerves
১৩) Glial cell that assists in production & circulation of CSF
১৪) Which insulates PNS axons?
১৫) Adult derivatives of metencephalon
১৬) Subdivision of prosencephalon
১৭) Primary visual area
১৮) Lateral surface of cerebrum is mainly supplied by
১৯) Cerebellar nuclei exclude
২০) Paravermisforms which lobe of cerebellum?
২১) Nucleus of hypothalamus involved in ADH synthesis
২২) Nucleus of hypothalamus involved in controlling circadian rhythms
২৩) L5 cord segment correspond which thoracic vertebrae?
২৪) Which cranial nerve helps in turning eyeball downward & laterally?
২৫) Parasympathetic supply relaxes
২৬) Normal cell in CSF
২৭) Uveal truct excludes
২৮) Which supplies nourishment to retina
২৯) Internal acoustic meatus transmits
৩০) Pacinian corpuscle is concerned with
৩১) Dermatome of umbilicus
৩২) Layer of epidermis only present in thick skin
৩৩) Which layer of epidermis contains Langerhans cell
৩৪) Most superficial layer of cerebram
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is molecular layer. The molecular layer (Layer I) is the most superficial layer of the cerebral cortex.

Layers of cerebral cortex (superficial → deep):

  1. Molecular layer (Layer I)

  2. External granular layer (Layer II)

  3. External pyramidal layer (Layer III)

  4. Internal granular layer (Layer IV)

  5. Internal pyramidal layer (Layer V)

  6. Multiform layer (Layer VI)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • External granular layer → Second layer of cerebral cortex.

  • External pyramidal layer → Third layer; contains pyramidal neurons.

  • Multiform layer → Deepest cortical layer (Layer VI).

High-yield cerebral cortex layers:

Molecular → External granular → External pyramidal → Internal granular → Internal pyramidal → Multiform

Exam pearl:
Most superficial cerebral cortex layer = Molecular layer (Layer I).

Anatomy-03.question: ৩৫) Anosmia is a disorder of which sensation?
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is smell. Anosmia means complete loss of the sense of smell.

Key points:

  • Sensation involved: Olfaction

  • Cranial nerve involved: Olfactory nerve (CN I)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Taste → Disorder is called ageusia (loss of taste).

  • Hearing → Disorder is called deafness/hearing loss.

  • Vision → Disorder is called blindness or visual impairment.

High-yield sensory disorders:

Sensation Loss of sensation
Smell Anosmia
Taste Ageusia
Hearing Deafness
Vision Blindness

Exam pearl:
Anosmia = loss of smell = Olfactory nerve (CN I).

Anatomy-03.question: ৩৬) Which type of papillae contains most taste bud
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is circumvallate papillae. Circumvallate (vallate) papillae contain the largest number of taste buds.

Key points:

  • Located at the junction of anterior 2/3 and posterior 1/3 of tongue

  • Usually 8–12 in number

  • Associated with von Ebner glands

  • Supplied mainly by glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Filiform papillae → Most numerous papillae; do not contain taste buds.

  • Fungiform papillae → Contain some taste buds, especially at the tip and sides of tongue.

  • Foliate papillae → Contain taste buds but are less prominent in humans.

High-yield tongue papillae:

Papilla Taste buds
Filiform Absent
Fungiform Present
Foliate Present
Circumvallate Most numerous taste buds

Exam pearl:
Maximum taste buds = Circumvallate papillae.

Anatomy-03.question: ৩৭) Signs of cerebellar lesion excludes
৩৮) Typical sweat gland is of... variety
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is eccrine sweat gland. The typical sweat gland of human skin is an eccrine (merocrine) gland.

Key points:

  • Eccrine glands are widely distributed throughout the skin

  • Produce watery sweat for:

    • Thermoregulation

    • Cooling of the body

  • Secretion occurs by merocrine mechanism (exocytosis)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Apocrine → Found mainly in axilla and anogenital regions; produces thicker secretion and becomes active after puberty.

  • Merocrine → A method of secretion, not a specific type of sweat gland; eccrine sweat glands use this mechanism.

  • Holocrine → Entire cell disintegrates during secretion; example: sebaceous glands.

High-yield sweat glands:

Gland Type Function
Eccrine Merocrine Thermoregulation
Apocrine Apocrine secretion Axillary/anogenital secretion
Sebaceous Holocrine Sebum production

Exam pearl:
Typical sweat gland = Eccrine (merocrine) gland.

Anatomy-03.question: ৩৯) Predominant cell type of epidermis
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is keratinocyte. Keratinocytes are the predominant cell type of the epidermis, making up about 90% of epidermal cells.

Functions of keratinocytes:

  • Produce keratin for protection

  • Form the main structural component of epidermis

  • Provide barrier against water loss and pathogens

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Melanocyte → Produces melanin pigment; located mainly in the stratum basale.

  • Langerhans cell → Antigen-presenting immune cell; mainly found in stratum spinosum.

  • Merkel cell → Mechanoreceptor involved in touch sensation; located in stratum basale.

High-yield epidermal cells:

Cell Function
Keratinocyte Most abundant epidermal cell; keratin production
Melanocyte Melanin production
Langerhans cell Immune defence
Merkel cell Touch sensation

Exam pearl:
Predominant cell of epidermis = Keratinocyte.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪০) The most abundant type of cerebral cortical neurons is the
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is pyramidal cell. Pyramidal neurons are the most abundant and characteristic neurons of the cerebral cortex.

Key points:

  • Large triangular cell body

  • Prominent apical dendrite extending toward the cortical surface

  • Long axon projecting to other cortical areas, brainstem, or spinal cord

  • Main excitatory projection neurons of the cerebral cortex

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Purkinje cell → Found in the cerebellar cortex, not cerebral cortex.

  • Stellate cell → Present in cerebral cortex (especially layer IV) but less abundant than pyramidal cells.

  • Fusiform cell → Found mainly in deeper cortical layers (layer VI).

High-yield cortical neurons:

Neuron Location
Pyramidal cell Most abundant neuron of cerebral cortex
Purkinje cell Cerebellar cortex
Stellate cell Cerebral cortex layer IV
Fusiform cell Cerebral cortex layer VI

Exam pearl:
Most abundant cerebral cortical neuron = Pyramidal cell.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪১) The substance of the tongue is made up chiefly of
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is skeletal muscle. The substance (bulk) of the tongue is mainly composed of interlacing bundles of skeletal muscle fibres.

Key points:

  • Tongue muscles are voluntary skeletal muscles

  • Arranged in:

    • Intrinsic muscles → Change shape of tongue

    • Extrinsic muscles → Move tongue position

  • Supplied mainly by hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Connective tissue → Provides support but does not form the main bulk.

  • Smooth muscle → Not present as the main muscle component of tongue.

  • Epithelial tissue → Covers the surface of the tongue.

High-yield tongue anatomy:

Component Main feature
Substance of tongue Skeletal muscle
Surface covering Stratified squamous epithelium
Motor nerve Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

Exam pearl:
Tongue is mainly made of skeletal muscle.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪২) Most numerous papillae of tongue
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is filiform papillae. Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae of the tongue.

Key points:

  • Most abundant type of tongue papillae

  • Thin, conical, keratinized projections

  • Provide mechanical function (help manipulate food)

  • Do not contain taste buds

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fungiform papillae → Mushroom-shaped; contain some taste buds.

  • Circumvallate papillae → Few in number (8–12) but contain the largest number of taste buds.

  • Foliate papillae → Contain taste buds but are less developed in humans.

High-yield tongue papillae:

Papilla Key feature
Filiform Most numerous; no taste buds
Fungiform Taste buds present
Circumvallate Most taste buds
Foliate Taste buds present

Exam pearl:
Most numerous papillae of tongue = Filiform papillae

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৩) The middle ear is placed within which bone?
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is temporal bone. The middle ear is located within the petrous part of the temporal bone.

Key points:

  • Middle ear cavity = tympanic cavity

  • Located in the petrous temporal bone

  • Contains:

    • Three auditory ossicles:

      • Malleus

      • Incus

      • Stapes

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Frontal bone → Forms forehead and anterior cranial fossa.

  • Parietal bone → Forms the roof and sides of the skull.

  • Occipital bone → Forms the posterior skull and foramen magnum.

High-yield ear anatomy:

Ear part Location
External ear Outside skull
Middle ear Petrous temporal bone
Inner ear Petrous temporal bone

Exam pearl:
Middle ear = Petrous part of temporal bone.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৪) The sensory organ of hearing is situated on
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is basilar membrane. The organ of Corti (sensory organ of hearing) is situated on the basilar membrane inside the cochlea.

Key points:

  • Organ of Corti = receptor organ for hearing

  • Located in the cochlear duct (scala media)

  • Rests on the basilar membrane

  • Contains inner and outer hair cells responsible for sound transduction

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Tectorial membrane → Overlies the organ of Corti and interacts with hair cells but does not support it.

  • Vestibular membrane (Reissner’s membrane) → Separates scala vestibuli from scala media.

  • Spiral membrane → Not the site of the organ of Corti.

High-yield inner ear anatomy:

Structure Function
Basilar membrane Supports organ of Corti (hearing receptor)
Tectorial membrane Stimulates hair cells
Vestibular membrane Maintains cochlear compartments

Exam pearl:
Sensory organ of hearing (Organ of Corti) = on basilar membrane.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৫) Which one is concerned with converting recent memory to long term memory?
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is hippocampus. The hippocampus is responsible for consolidation of recent memory into long-term memory.

Key points:

  • Located in the medial temporal lobe

  • Essential for:

    • Formation of new memories

    • Conversion of short-term memory → long-term memory

    • Spatial memory

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Amygdala → Involved in emotional processing, especially fear and emotional memory.

  • Putamen → Part of basal ganglia; involved in motor control and habit learning.

  • Pallidum (globus pallidus) → Part of basal ganglia; regulates movement.

High-yield memory structures:

Structure Function
Hippocampus Recent memory → long-term memory consolidation
Amygdala Emotional memory
Cerebral cortex Long-term memory storage
Basal ganglia Procedural/habit memory

Exam pearl:
Conversion of recent memory to long-term memory = Hippocampus.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৬) Filum terminale is a thin fibrous cord form by
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is pia mater. The filum terminale is a thin fibrous extension of pia mater that anchors the spinal cord inferiorly.

Key points:

  • Extends from the conus medullaris to the coccyx

  • Provides support and fixation of the spinal cord

  • Has two parts:

    • Filum terminale internum → Pia mater extension within dural sac

    • Filum terminale externum (coccygeal ligament) → Covered by dura mater

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Dura mater → Forms the dural sac and contributes to the external covering of filum terminale externum.

  • Arachnoid mater → Does not form the filum terminale.

  • All layers of meninges → Incorrect; mainly derived from pia mater.

High-yield spinal meninges:

Structure Origin
Filum terminale Pia mater
Dural sac Dura mater
Subarachnoid space Between arachnoid and pia; contains CSF

Exam pearl:
Filum terminale = extension of pia mater.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৭) Two cerebral hemispheres are connected to each other by the
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is corpus callosum. The corpus callosum is the largest commissural fibre bundle that connects the two cerebral hemispheres.

Key points:

  • Contains millions of myelinated nerve fibres

  • Allows communication between the right and left cerebral hemispheres

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Internal capsule → Contains projection fibres connecting the cerebral cortex with brainstem and spinal cord.

  • Uncinate fasciculus → Connects the frontal lobe with the temporal lobe of the same hemisphere.

  • Cingulum → Association fibre tract connecting parts of the limbic lobe within the same hemisphere.

High-yield white matter fibres:

Type Example
Commissural fibres Corpus callosum (connects both hemispheres)
Projection fibres Internal capsule
Association fibres Uncinate fasciculus, cingulum

Exam pearl:
Connection between two cerebral hemispheres = Corpus callosum.

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৮) Broca’s motor speech area (Broadman area)-
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is Brodmann areas 44 and 45. Broca’s area is the motor speech area responsible for speech production.

Key points:

  • Location: Dominant frontal lobe (usually left hemisphere)

  • Function: Motor planning and production of speech

  • Lesion causes: Expressive (Broca) aphasia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Area 4 → Primary motor cortex; controls voluntary movements.

  • Areas 6, 8 → Premotor and frontal eye field areas.

  • Areas 3, 1, 2 → Primary somatosensory cortex.

High-yield Brodmann areas:

Function Area
Primary motor cortex 4
Premotor cortex 6
Frontal eye field 8
Broca’s motor speech area 44, 45
Primary somatosensory cortex 3, 1, 2
Primary visual cortex 17

Exam pearl:
Broca’s area = Brodmann area 44 & 45 (dominant inferior frontal gyrus).

Anatomy-03.question: ৪৯) Oculomotor, Abducent & ophthalmic nerve passes through
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is superior orbital fissure. The oculomotor nerve (CN III), abducent nerve (CN VI), and ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve (CN V1) pass through the superior orbital fissure.

Structures passing through superior orbital fissure:

  • CN III (Oculomotor nerve)

  • CN IV (Trochlear nerve)

  • CN V1 (Ophthalmic division)

  • CN VI (Abducent nerve)

  • Superior ophthalmic vein

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Foramen rotundum → Transmits maxillary nerve (CN V2).

  • Foramen ovale → Transmits mandibular nerve (CN V3).

  • Internal acoustic meatus → Transmits facial nerve (CN VII) and vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).

High-yield skull foramina:

Foramen Nerve
Superior orbital fissure CN III, IV, V1, VI
Foramen rotundum CN V2
Foramen ovale CN V3
Internal acoustic meatus CN VII, VIII

Exam pearl:
“SOF = 3, 4, V1, 6” → Superior orbital fissure.

Anatomy-03.question: ৫০) Origin of vestibulocochlear nerve
Anatomy-03.exp:
The correct answer is ponto-medullary junction. The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) emerges from the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle near the pontomedullary junction.

Key points:

  • Cranial nerve: CN VIII

  • Components:

    • Cochlear nerve → Hearing

    • Vestibular nerve → Balance and equilibrium

  • Enters the temporal bone through the internal acoustic meatus

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Midbrain → Origin of CN III and CN IV.

  • Pons → Origin of several cranial nerves including CN V, but CN VIII emerges lower at the pontomedullary junction.

  • Medulla → Origin of CN IX, X, XI, XII.

High-yield cranial nerve emergence:

Brainstem level Cranial nerves
Midbrain CN III, IV
Pons CN V
Ponto-medullary junction CN VI, VII, VIII
Medulla CN IX, X, XI, XII

Exam pearl:
Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) → pontomedullary junction.
